claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials can combine very high strength with substantial impact-induced chemical energy release.
The target refractory HEAs suffer from limited plasticity under mechanical loading.
The target refractory HEAs exhibit strain localization and nonuniform deformability.
Cyclic deformation with controlled cooling can produce a gradient microstructure in a refractory HEA.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment can generate ultrafine coherent nanoprecipitates along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Grain-size gradients and nanoprecipitation are recognized strategies for improving strength–ductility synergy in compositionally complex alloys.
Nanoprecipitates can provide precipitation strengthening and progressive multistage strain hardening that delays localized plastic instability.
Uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates in a gradient refractory-HEA microstructure will impede localized dislocation motion and arrest strain concentration.
The engineered microstructure will increase uniform ductility and produce more homogeneous deformation under dynamic loading.
The treated refractory HEA will retain tensile strength comparable to the untreated baseline.
The treatment will preserve impact-induced energy release comparable to that of the untreated alloy.
Refractory energetic HEAs can retain high strength and substantial fracture strain during dynamic loading at approximately 3000 s−1.
The beneficial effect requires precise control of precipitate size, precipitate distribution, and the gradient structure.

Departures from the required precipitate and gradient structure may eliminate the ductility benefit or reduce strength and energy release, particularly at untested extreme temperatures or strain rates.
The magnitude of the ductility improvement and the strength–deformability balance remain uncertain pending systematic experiments.
